title: A hundred moons, a thousand suns
hookLine: one of his saloks says all is darkness without the Guru
carry: the guru's light shows the way

cards: A snowfield at midday. Light pours down from the sky and bounces back off the snow until everything is one bright white. You can see perfectly well.
But the trail markers are buried, and you have no idea which way the path goes. Plenty of light. No direction.
The light that fills your eyes and the light that shows you the way are not the same thing. Guru Angad has a salok built on exactly that difference, and the picture is enormous.

teach.h: A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.
teach.b: The salok sits in Asa di Var, the ballad sung in the morning at the gurdwara, marked Mahala two.
In paraphrase: if a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns appeared, even with all that light, without the Guru there would be pitch darkness. Stop on the size of that.
A hundred moons, a thousand suns, more light than any sky has held, and still not enough. So he can't mean light for the eyes.

teach.h: THE LIGHT THAT SHOWS THE WAY.
teach.b: He means the light that shows a person where they are and which way to go: what's true, what's ego, what's worth a life. In Sikh teaching, that light comes from the Guru. And who is the Guru?

For Sikhs, the Gurus in their lifetimes, and now the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word itself. Earlier this year, in the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak said the Word is the Guru. Guru Angad's salok shows what that Guru does.
It doesn't add brightness to a world already full of it. It turns a different kind of darkness into sight.

teach.h: NOT MORE LIGHT, BUT GUIDED SIGHT.
teach.b: It's easy to assume more is the answer: more information, more options, more light on the screen. This verse quietly says no.
You can be flooded with light and still be in the dark. What changes things isn't how much you can see, but whether something guides your seeing. That's today's line: the Guru's light shows the way.

how: Sikhs hear this salok when Asa di Var is sung in the morning at the gurdwara, and Sikh teachers use it to speak of the Guru's guidance, through the Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: what does “the guru as light” mean?
o: the guidance that shows the way, beyond any sun
the halo painted around the Gurus' heads
a lamp kept burning beside the scripture

games.q: the salok, piece by piece: tap the pairs.

s: in the salok, a hundred moons and a thousand suns finally end the darkness
it says even with all that light, without the Guru there would be pitch darkness.
the salok is found in Asa di Var, marked Mahala two
it's one of Guru Angad's saloks in the morning ballad.
the light the salok means is light for the eyes
it piles up more light than any sky holds and says it isn't enough; it means the light that shows the way.

games.q: a hundred moons rise and a thousand suns appear. what does Guru Angad's salok say about the dark?
o: without the Guru, it's still pitch dark.
games.why: even with all that light, he says, without the Guru there would be pitch darkness.

practice: Remember a time you had plenty of information and still didn't know which way to go, then remember what helped you see: a teacher, a line from a text, a parent, a friend, a hard lesson.
Hold that one clearly, with thanks, for a few slow breaths. If you pray, thank the Guru and say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: The Guru as light. Guru Angad's picture: a hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru, the light that shows the way. Today's word.

orig.note: the Guru: for Sikhs, the Gurus and now the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: the Guru's light shows the way. A hundred moons can't do what the Guru does. Go gently.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, salok Mahala 2, Ang 463 (if a hundred moons rose and a thousand suns, without the Guru there would be pitch darkness)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali, Sidh Gosht, Ang 943 (the Word is the Guru)
